title: Penal substitution and the Life-Giving Cross
subtitle: The Cross heals and it also pays; what the Fathers refuse is a God who must be bought before he can love.
summary: Did Christ die to satisfy a judge, or to heal a disease? The Fathers refuse the choice. They keep the debt, the ransom, and the curse borne, and they insist the payment works by union with our nature rather than by a verdict pronounced over it. Ignatius, Irenaeus, Athanasius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom, with the question Gregory asks out loud at Pascha: to whom was the Blood offered?

essay.text: Before this is an argument it is a bedside question. Someone kneels in the dark before confession, or sits with a diagnosis, or walks home from a funeral, and wants to know what God is toward him at that moment. The answer most of us absorb from the culture around us is a courtroom: a Judge whose anger had to be spent somewhere, and a Son who stepped into its path. That picture is held by many devout people, and it has kept some of them in the faith. But it leaves a person managing his standing rather than being made new, and when the fear returns at three in the morning he has nothing to say to it except that the payment should still be good. The Fathers offer something else, and it is not less serious about sin. It is more serious.

Scripture will not let us choose between the two vocabularies. Christ is the physician who came for the sick, and he is the ransom given for many. By his stripes we are healed, and the handwriting that was against us is blotted out and nailed to his cross. The Fathers use all of it. Athanasius writes that the debt was satisfied. Cyril of Jerusalem says the sentence of God was not simply cancelled. Chrysostom says the Righteous One was made a sinner so that sinners might be made righteous, and says in the same homily that the One who did no wrong was suffered to be punished for those who had done wrong. So the Orthodox difficulty with penal substitution has never been a difficulty with sacrificial or legal words, which are apostolic. It is a difficulty with a particular system assembled out of them, and the difference is worth stating slowly rather than shouting.
The sentence and the sickness are one wound

We inherit from Adam a nature that runs down toward corruption, and a world in which death has the last word. What passes to us is that corruption and that mortality, not a personal share in Adam's guilt. And death is not only a sickness. It is also the just word God spoke over sin. That is why healing language by itself underdescribes what happened at Golgotha. A cure that left the sentence in force would not be a cure, and a pardon that left the corruption in place would leave us still dying. Cyril of Jerusalem sets the dilemma out and then refuses both horns of it: God in his truth could have destroyed all men, or in his loving-kindness could have cancelled the sentence, and instead "He preserved both the truth of His sentence, and the exercise of His loving-kindness." The Church has therefore never been shy of saying that Christ bore what was ours to bear. What she guards is who was doing the bearing, and why.
To whom was the Blood offered

Gregory the Theologian asks that question at Pascha, in front of the whole congregation, and he will not take either of the obvious answers. If the ransom was paid to the evil one, that is an outrage, for then the robber receives God himself as his fee. If it was paid to the Father, then how, since it was not the Father who held us in bondage. His conclusion is exact: "the Father accepts Him, but neither asked for Him nor demanded Him." The debt is real, and Irenaeus says plainly whose it is: "we were debtors to none other but to Him whose commandment we had transgressed at the beginning." So what falls away is not the debt, the ransom, or the propitiation. What falls away is the picture of a Father who cannot love until he has been paid, and with it any suggestion that the Son is merciful while the Father is not. A synod at Constantinople, sitting in 1156 and 1157, put the same thing in conciliar form: the one sacrifice is offered to the whole Trinity, by the Son who as God receives it together with the Father and the Spirit. There is no buyer and no seller inside God.
What is not assumed is not healed

Ignatius, writing on the road to the lions, already calls Christ "one Physician." Gregory the Theologian gives the rule that makes the image precise: "that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved." Salvation happens by union, which is why it could never have been transacted at a distance from our nature. Irenaeus shows the shape of the cure: a tree undone by a tree, disobedience undone by obedience, the whole line of Adam begun again in Christ. And Athanasius holds the two idioms together in a single breath. The Word "satisfied the debt by His death," and by that same offering "put away death from all His peers," clothing our nature with incorruption. The payment is not a credit posted to an account we never see. It is our own flesh, taken by God, put to death, and raised imperishable. That is also why the reckoning does not end on Friday. The Church sings that he trampled down death by death, and that hymn is the conclusion of the argument, not a change of subject.

Orthodox teachers, including recent ones, use satisfaction language without embarrassment. The Russian word is udovletvorenie, and the catechism of St Philaret of Moscow answers this exact question by holding two things together: the death of Christ both satisfies the justice that had condemned us, and wins a merit without limit out of which we are given pardon of our sins and the strength to overcome sin and death. Held that way, satisfaction is not a rival to healing. It describes how the road was cleared, how the guard set at the gate of Eden was withdrawn so that the way to the tree of life stood open again. The line falls in three places. First, when the wrath of the Father becomes the obstacle that love has to get around, rather than his love being the thing that sends the Son. Second, when justification is reduced to a verdict spoken over a man who is left inwardly untouched, whereas the Fathers mean by it both the forgiveness of sins and an actual renewing of him, worked out over a life and never without his own willing. Third, when the Cross is made a transaction between an angry Person and a merciful one, which divides the undivided God. Refuse those three and every sacrificial word in the Bible may be kept, and kept gladly. And here is what it means at the analogion: you are not being retried. You are being treated, by the Physician who has already borne the sentence, and who bore it because he loved you first.

florilegium.author: St Ignatius of Antioch
florilegium.text: There is one Physician who is possessed both of flesh and spirit; both made and not made; God existing in flesh; true life in death; both of Mary and of God; first passible and then impassible.
florilegium.gloss: The earliest voice in this study, and it is a medical one. Ignatius names Christ the one Physician long before any system of atonement is built, and the sentence closes by naming that Physician as Jesus Christ our Lord.

florilegium.author: St Irenaeus of Lyons
florilegium.text: And not by the aforesaid things alone has the Lord manifested Himself, but [He has done this] also by means of His passion. For doing away with [the effects of] that disobedience of man which had taken place at the beginning by the occasion of a tree, He became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross; rectifying that disobedience which had occurred by reason of a tree, through that obedience which was [wrought out] upon the tree [of the cross]. Now He would not have come to do away, by means of that same [image], the disobedience which had been incurred towards our Maker if He proclaimed another Father. But inasmuch as it was by these things that we disobeyed God, and did not give credit to His word, so was it also by these same that He brought in obedience and consent as respects His Word; by which things He clearly shows forth God Himself, whom indeed we had offended in the first Adam, when he did not perform His commandment. In the second Adam, however, we are reconciled, being made obedient even unto death. For we were debtors to none other but to Him whose commandment we had transgressed at the beginning.
florilegium.gloss: Recapitulation in a single paragraph: a tree undone by a tree, disobedience undone by obedience. Irenaeus keeps the word debtors, and he is precise about the creditor. The debt was owed to God, not to the devil.

florilegium.author: St Irenaeus of Lyons
florilegium.text: Now this being is the Creator (Demiurgus), who is, in respect of His love, the Father; but in respect of His power, He is Lord; and in respect of His wisdom, our Maker and Fashioner; by transgressing whose commandment we became His enemies. And therefore in the last times the Lord has restored us into friendship through His incarnation, having become the Mediator between God and men; propitiating indeed for us the Father against whom we had sinned, and cancelling (consolatus) our disobedience by His own obedience; conferring also upon us the gift of communion with, and subjection to, our Maker.
florilegium.gloss: Propitiation and healing in one clause. Christ propitiates the Father, and the means is an obedience that cancels our disobedience. The end of it is not an acquittal but communion with our Maker.

florilegium.author: St Athanasius the Great
florilegium.work: On the Incarnation of the Word
florilegium.text: Whence, by offering unto death the body He Himself had taken, as an offering and sacrifice free from any stain, straightway He put away death from all His peers by the offering of an equivalent. For being over all, the Word of God naturally by offering His own temple and corporeal instrument for the life of all satisfied the debt by His death.
florilegium.gloss: Athanasius is not working with a forensic scheme, and he still writes that the debt was satisfied and that the offering was an equivalent. The same sentences say why it works. The body offered is our own nature, taken by the Word, so the payment and the cure are one act.

florilegium.author: St Cyril of Jerusalem
florilegium.text: For we were enemies of God through sin, and God had appointed the sinner to die. There must needs therefore have happened one of two things; either that God, in His truth, should destroy all men, or that in His loving-kindness He should cancel the sentence. But behold the wisdom of God; He preserved both the truth of His sentence, and the exercise of His loving-kindness. Christ took our sins in His body on the tree, that we by His death might die to sin, and live unto righteousness.
florilegium.gloss: The clearest patristic statement of the both/and. God does not suspend his sentence in order to be merciful, and he does not enforce it in order to be true. At the Cross he is both at once.

florilegium.author: St Gregory the Theologian
florilegium.work: Oration 45, The Second Oration on Easter
florilegium.text: Now we are to examine another fact and dogma, neglected by most people, but in my judgment well worth enquiring into. To Whom was that Blood offered that was shed for us, and why was It shed? I mean the precious and famous Blood of our God and High priest and Sacrifice. We were detained in bondage by the Evil One, sold under sin, and receiving pleasure in exchange for wickedness. Now, since a ransom belongs only to him who holds in bondage, I ask to whom was this offered, and for what cause? If to the Evil One, fie upon the outrage! If the robber receives ransom, not only from God, but a ransom which consists of God Himself, and has such an illustrious payment for his tyranny, a payment for whose sake it would have been right for him to have left us alone altogether. But if to the Father, I ask first, how? For it was not by Him that we were being oppressed; and next, On what principle did the Blood of His Only begotten Son delight the Father, Who would not receive even Isaac, when he was being offered by his Father, but changed the sacrifice, putting a ram in the place of the human victim? Is it not evident that the Father accepts Him, but neither asked for Him nor demanded Him; but on account of the Incarnation, and because Humanity must be sanctified by the Humanity of God, that He might deliver us Himself, and overcome the tyrant, and draw us to Himself by the mediation of His Son, Who also arranged this to the honour of the Father, Whom it is manifest that He obeys in all things?
florilegium.gloss: Gregory asks out loud the question the modern debate assumes it has answered, and refuses both easy replies. The Blood is not a fee paid to the devil, and the Father is not a creditor who demanded it. The Father accepts what love offers.

florilegium.author: St Gregory the Theologian
florilegium.work: Oration 45, The Second Oration on Easter
florilegium.text: We needed an Incarnate God, a God put to death, that we might live. We were put to death together with Him, that we might be cleansed; we rose again with Him because we were put to death with Him; we were glorified with Him, because we rose again with Him.
florilegium.gloss: The same oration that refuses to make the Cross a fee paid to an offended party insists that we needed a God put to death. Nothing is being softened. The death is necessary, and it is necessary because we die in it with him.

florilegium.author: St Gregory the Theologian
florilegium.text: For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved. If only half Adam fell, then that which Christ assumes and saves may be half also; but if the whole of his nature fell, it must be united to the whole nature of Him that was begotten, and so be saved as a whole.
florilegium.gloss: The rule that governs everything else. Salvation happens by union, so whatever Christ does not take up he does not cure. A payment made outside our nature could not have reached us.

florilegium.author: St John Chrysostom
florilegium.reference: Homily 11, on 2 Corinthians 5:21 (NPNF First Series, vol. 12)
florilegium.text: "For the righteous," says he, "He made a sinner; that He might make the sinners righteous." Yea rather, he said not even so, but what was greater far; for the word he employed is not the habit, but the quality itself.
florilegium.gloss: Substitutionary language is native to the Greek Fathers, and Chrysostom preaches it here on 2 Corinthians 5:21. What he does not do is make the exchange a fiction, since he insists Paul means the quality itself and not a reputation.

florilegium.author: St John Chrysostom
florilegium.reference: Homily 11, on 2 Corinthians 5:21 (NPNF First Series, vol. 12)
florilegium.text: For had He achieved nothing but done only this, think how great a thing it were to give His Son for those that had outraged Him. But now He has both well achieved mighty things, and besides, has suffered Him that did no wrong to be punished for those who had done wrong.
florilegium.gloss: The strongest penal note in this study, and it is Chrysostom preaching rather than a later system arguing. He says outright that the One who did no wrong was suffered to be punished for those who had. Set beside Gregory's Pascha question it shows the range the Fathers keep: a real punishment borne, and no creditor inside God demanding it.

scripture.note: He bore our griefs, and by his wounds we are healed. The one passage that holds bearing and healing together, which is why both parties quote it.
They that are whole need not a physician. The Lord's own account of why he came.
A ransom for many. The word is the Lord's, which is why the Fathers keep it and argue only about to whom it is paid.
The two Adams, the ground of recapitulation and of Irenaeus' whole reading of the Cross.
Made him to be sin for us. Chrysostom reads it as a real exchange rather than a change of reputation.
Made a curse for us. The curse is borne by the sinless One, and the Fathers describe him as taking it up rather than having it charged to him.
The handwriting blotted out and the principalities triumphed over, in one act. Debt cancelled and enemy defeated are the same event.
Through death he destroys him that had the power of death. The victory idiom, in the apostolic text itself.
